explanation: Fires on a pronoun (mostly possessive his/her/their/my/your, or a subject pronoun starting a relative clause like 'a girl he had', 'the team he's') placed right after a copula/linking verb or a noun, where it marks someone's relationship or role ('X is her coach', 'Henry's my dog', 'asked her to be his'). Strongest in predicative 'is/was/be + possessive' role constructions. Generic pronouns in other positions fire weakly; non-pronouns barely at all.

Fires mainly on 'the' (and similar function tokens) that come after verbs or nouns of improving, increasing or reducing an outcome or rate ('improving conversion rates and the chances', 'lower the quality', 'enhance the efficiency', 'lower bound on the failure probability'), and also on sentence-final periods and words like 'median'/'5-year' in clinical or statistical outcome prose. One top example far outweighs the rest; most other examples are weak.

Fires on the second or later subword piece of a long or uncommon identifier or word: CamelCase class names in code (SelectListItem, UIImagePickerController, TextInputType), dotted package parts in import lines (.Intent, .os), and the inner pieces of rare names or words (B-ingham-ton, Phil-ippi, pilgr-ims, babys-itters, McCorm-ack). What matters is that the token continues a word rather than starting one.

Fires on joining punctuation inside compound tokens: hyphens in compound words and URL slugs ('now-destroyed', 'super-elite', 'in-5-minutes'), apostrophes in French elisions (l'année), the Japanese middle dot, slashes and '+' in URLs, ' *)' in Objective-C signatures, and broken Devanagari bytes. Ordinary spaces and words give at most weak activation.

Mixed. The clearest group is 'of' inside organization names (Society of, School of, National Association of), plus 'personal' in 'personal computer/digital assistant'. Other strong examples are unrelated: 'were' after a plural subject in methods text, '-old' in ages, 'flight' instructor, 'Students', 'make'.

Fires on the colon or the space just before a value in CSS property declarations (width/height/left/min-width: 0), and less strongly on similar key-value or assignment separators in code and config (=, ":" in JSON, ' =' assignments, RewriteRule). Prose fires weakly or not at all.

Fires on the second or later subword token of a word written in ALL CAPS (headlines, surnames in legal captions, place names in addresses: BIRMING-HAM, G-IL-BERT, SN-OW, LE-ADER), and on the second word of a run of capital letters ('OUT OF', 'I LOVE'). Strongest at the start of a capitalized headline or name; lowercase text does not fire.

Mixed. Recurring pieces are 'cart' in 'shopping cart', 'stents', and second subword pieces of names or terms (ECMAS-cript, C-ort, Greg-ory, tr-avis, wholes-aler, CJK characters), along with unrelated tokens like '\includegraphics', 'bottom line', 'By the time'. No single shared feature is clear.

Fires at the start of a Stack Overflow-style question, on the first few tokens of the title or opening body after 'Q:' ('I am trying', 'Here is my code', 'not working', 'works fine'). Especially strong on 'am' in 'I am', 'my' in 'my code', and 'fine'/'not' in descriptions of code working or failing. Programming-help questions only; other text fires weakly.

Fires on a word piece that completes a fixed multiword phrase or standard string: '/android' in the xmlns URL, 'assistance' in 'ineffective assistance of counsel', 'Cuts' in Tax Cuts and Jobs Act, 'soluble' before thrombomodulin, 'editor' in 'Letter to the editor', 'more' in the Apache license header, 'NATURALIZATION'. The token is highly predictable from the boilerplate before it.

No clear pattern. Top tokens include an SVG path letter, Devanagari bytes, 'message', 't in didn't, closing braces, indentation, digits in math expressions, 'coated', 'ceramic', '||', 'char'. They share no evident feature.

Fires on the non-first piece of a multi-token proper name, acronym or technical term (Alcat-raz, receiver operating characteristic, cognitive-behavioral, W-MS, OS-HA, NMD-A, Lend-Lease, Dead Sea, National Register of Historic Places, Phase III). The strength comes from finishing a known compound name or term; the token alone matters less than its position inside that entity.

No coherent pattern. Strong examples include 'attributes' in assembly-info boilerplate, 'License' in Apache License, hyphens inside UUIDs, 'burning', 'you', 'utilized', 'family', 'law', 'Perfect', 'versión'. Some lean toward boilerplate continuations, but many do not.

Fires on function words and verb forms in Spanish or Portuguese text, especially mid-sentence verbs and connectives (como, será, es, foi, tiveram, até, que, marquei). It fires more weakly on 'de'/'del' inside Spanish names in English text. English and other languages do not fire.

Fires at structural boundaries where a block of code or text ends and a new one begins: closing lines and indentation before '})' or '}', 'End Sub', '</head>', 'HEADER END', '====' separator lines after license headers, and the first token of a new section ('A:', 'I. BACKGROUND'). Ordinary prose fires weakly.

Fires on the first word (or an early word) of a new sentence or clause that moves the discussion on, often a determiner or pronoun referring back ('This one is', 'These frames', 'These bats', 'We must', 'and although'), in expository or blog prose. The context of starting a follow-up statement matters more than the token itself.

Mixed, with no unified feature. Some groups recur: 'Janeiro' in 'Rio de Janeiro', 'import (' in Go files, '.php' in URLs or filenames, the second pieces of package names (supertest, restful), and surname pieces. Unrelated tokens such as 'as', 'in', 'package', 'Oslo' also fire strongly.

Fires on object-oriented class or interface declaration syntax in code: Objective-C '@interface'/'@property' and protocol names after NSObject, PHP '__construct', 'interface', 'namespace', and the indentation that opens the first member of a class body. Strongest right after a class declaration header. Prose does not fire.

No clear unifying pattern. Strong examples include 'Message' in '-----Original Message-----', 'Christ', 'Up' in 'Team Up', Greek and Cyrillic word pieces, 'of', 'aspirin', 'treks', 'e.g', 'Kaiserslautern' pieces. They mix email boilerplate, mid-word pieces and function words.

Fires on terms from immigration and visas (H-1B, visa, Deferred Action, naturalized) and on biomedical growth factors and cytokines (SCF, chemokine, VEGF, FGF, growth factor), plus words from grant applications ('career development', CAREER award, 'This project'). Two to three distinct themes; the token's content matters.

Fires on 'the', 'of', 'a', 'an' or 'to' in formal definitional or locational phrases, the kind that fix where something belongs ('in the genus', 'region of Vietnam', 'incorporated under the laws', 'is an autosomal', 'licensed under the'), typical of encyclopedia, legal or abstract-introduction prose. Function words in casual text fire weakly.
